Name: Flexle: Flexible level-based sampling
Content: Stochastic simulation of agent-based models requires efficient sampling from weighted distributions that constantly change their probability weights based on the simulation's events. Flexle (flexible, binary-level rejection sampling) is a Julia package for high performance sampling from discrete distributions under the constraint of being able to quickly modify said distributions.

Name: Opqua v1.0: Evo-epidemiological simulation in Python
Content:
Opqua is a flexible simulation framework that explicitly links epidemiology to sequence evolution and selection. Opqua stochastically simulates pathogens with distinct, evolving genotypes that spread through populations of hosts which can have specific immune profiles. Opqua is a useful tool to test out scenarios, explore hypotheses, make predictions, and teach about the relationship between pathogen evolution and epidemiology.

Since its creation in 2020 and publication in 2022 (before the start of MsEE Lab), the original Opqua project has given rise to other, more advanced simulation frameworks. The Python implementation of the framework is no longer being maintained.

Name: jOpqua: Evo-immuno-epidemiological simulation in Julia
Content:
jOpqua is a revised, Julia language implementation of the Opqua evo-epidemiological simulation package. Like its predecessor, it is a flexible simulation framework that explicitly links epidemiology to sequence evolution and selection. It stochastically simulates pathogens with distinct, evolving genotypes that spread through populations of hosts which can have specific immune profiles.

Unlike its Python-language predecessor, jOpqua is powerful enough to handle simulations with hundreds of thousands or even millions of individual agents. It is also significantly more flexible and customizable, particularly in its handling of host immunity to pathogens. It is still under active development.

Name: Intrahost pathogen evolution algorithm
Content: When a pathogen's infection-transmission cycle is short and immunity is protective of infection, as in influenza virus infection, its evolution can be approximated as occuring on an inter-host basis. However, many pathogens have longer infection timelines during which immunity and/or treatment provide changing selection pressures, as in HIV, chronic SARS-CoV-2 infection, malaria, or bacterial infections like tuberculosis. To make accurate predictions of evolutionary likelihood in these situations, evo-epidemiological simulations must approximate intrahost evolution more carefully. We are exploring simulation algorithms to be able to do this efficiently and accurately at scale.

Name: What determines antimalarial resistance evolution?
Content: Antimalarial resistance evolution threatens to undo decades of progress against malaria. Understanding the determinants of this evolution can be a valuable asset when designing public health policy. Resistance to antifolates is determined by a well-studied set of mutations, and models of this evolution led by Brandon Ogbunugafor and others (e.g. here and here) have shed light on this question. To be able to accurately simulate antimalarial resistance evolution at the population level, we must now use these well-studied fitness landscapes and intrahost simulations to inform multiscale simulations.

Name: What shapes influenza antigenic cluster evolution?
Content: Influenza virus evolution is dictated by evasion of host immunity. Interestingly, even though this evolution happens at a steady, continuous pace at the nucleotide level, it is punctuated by large jumps at the level of antigenic distance. These jumps separate influenza strains into "antigenic clusters" and determine how effective vaccines and preexisting immunity are against a given strain, thus making them crucial to designing interventions against the disease. Using data from high-throughput library strategies developed by the Schmidt lab and others as well as evo-epidemiological simulations, we explore the factors that determine virus evolution through these clusters.

Name: What determines likelihood of zoonotic pathogen spillover?
Content: Zoonotic pathogens can be a devastating threat to society, as seen multiple times over human history. Understanding the likelihood of a zoonotic spillover event leading to pandemic proportions requires multiscale simulation tools that take into account fitness landscapes, population characteristics, and random chance. We aim to use simulations to quantify this likelihood in different scenarios.

Name: Evolutionary robustness optimization for synthetic therapeutics
Content: Synthetic biology allows us to design cells that act as "living therapeutics" capable of complex, adaptable behaviors that single molecules can't achieve. This is the focus of our friends and colleagues at the Harimoto Lab at Cornell CBE. In collaboration with them, MsEE Lab explores design strategies to make these living therapeutics more evolutionarily stable.

Name: glOpqua: Host-to-global scale evo-epidemiological simulation
Content: Agent-based evo-epidemiological simulations can provide insight into the fundamental principles of pathogen evolution and make predictions about local-level microevolution in specific environments. To make accurate predictions of evolution in global pathogen systems, we must develop global-scale simulation techniques that interface with lower-scale simulation algorithms. glOpqua is one attempt at doing this by creating global-scale deterministic models informed by lower-scale stochastic models.

Name: Evolutionary forecast landscapes
Content: A central concept in evolutionary biology is the fitness landscape, the map describing how genetic sequences are related to evolutionary success, often understood as improved protein function. However, fitness does not directly correlate to the likelihood a genotype is observed: surrounding lanscape topology, mutation supply, and population characteristics all affect  which genotypes are accessible regardless of their fitness. Because of this, we can picture a different kind of landscape that maps the forecasted likelihood of genotypes occurring for a given population throughout future time, with measures of uncertainty in these forecasts. These evolutionary forecast landscapes can help design more robust interventions anywhere we engineer biology.

Name: What determines stochastic tunneling in evolution?
Content:
Fitness valleys occur when two genotypes conferring high levels of fitness are separated by mutant genotypes with low levels of fitness. They can be the consequence of epistasis between deleterous mutations which, when combined, provide a fitness advantage. We see fitness valleys occur in the evolution of pathogen drug resistance, host adaptation, and immune evasion. The process of evolving across a fitness valley from one peak to another is known as stochastic tunneling. We are interested in how epidemiological contexts can shape competition and clonal interference between pathogens to hamper this stochastic tunneling towards novel traits separated by fitness valleys.

In previous work, we use Opqua to study determinants of evolution across fitness valleys. We confirm that competition can limit evolution in high-transmission environments and find that low transmission, host mobility, and complex pathogen life cycles facilitate reaching new adaptive peaks through population bottlenecks and decoupling of selective pressures.

Name: What are the minimal key events that describe the evolution of a population?
Content: The experimental, question-based counterpart of a minimal simulation algorithm for population evolution. We plan to observe synthetic, evolving populations in the lab, identify key events that change or determine an evolutionary trajectory, and recreate and validate these events using the synthetic biology-based experimental control we have over the system.

Name: How do fitness prediction models fail and succeed?
Content: Machine learning models of fitness effects make predictions of the impact that specific mutations will have on protein fitness. Although many are successful at predicting the effects of single mutations, their effectiveness decreases as mutations compound, particularly due to the effects of epistasis. Quantifying the degree to which this discrepancy happens is difficult, given that we don't have access to the "ground truth" data: the real fitness landscapes that generate the sequences used to train these models. Because of this, we are using mechanistic simulations of evolution such as jOpqua to generate synthetic sequence from known "synthetic ground truth" fitness landscapes that we have full control over. By using these synthetic datasets to evaluate the performance of different machine learning architectures and training data sampling strategies, we can understand the limits of fitness effect predictions and design more effective ways to build predictive models.

Name: Fluorescent reporters of evolutionary trajectories
Content: Observing evolutionary trajectories in experiments commonly requires sequencing, which occurs outside of the experimental timeline besides being costly at scale. We are building synthetic circuits to report on trajectories through controlled fitness landscapes using fluorescent reporters in real experimental time.

Name: Synthetic circuits for cancer therapy that suppress the evolution of resistance
Content: When developing combination therapies for cancer and infectious disease, we often look for synergistic interactions that increase the strength of therapy. However, this creates a fitness landscape that facilitates the stepwise evolution of resistance to treatment, since mutants with resistance to one treatment will survive better than wild-type cells. Hyper-antagonistic of suppression therapy has been proposed as an alternative approach in which mutants with resistance to one treatment are less successful than the wild-type, but requires carefully tuned parameters to be successful. Synthetic biology allows us to design therapy strategies with high flexibilbity by uncoupling sensing of targets from mechanisms of cell killing. Using synthetic biological circuits, we aim to design cancer therapy that is more robust to the evolution of resistance.

Name: How do geographic inequalities in vaccination distribution affect the evolution of immune evasion?
Content: One of the key questions in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic was how the limieted supply of vaccines should be distributed within and between countries. Strategies that aim to minimize short-term spread overall or in a particular region may not align well with those aimed at reducing pathogen evolution in the medium and long term, leading to immune evasion that eventually renders the vaccine ineffective everywhere. We are interested in understanding vaccine distribution strategies that optimize for epidemiological and evolutionary control.

Name: How do tradeoffs in immune breadth and affinity shape pathogen evolution across host species such as bats?
Content: The breadth and affinity of antibody responses often trade off with each other, and the balance can be different in different organisms. It may help explain why some hosts, sucha s bats, are common sources of zoonotic infections. We collaborate with the Plowright Lab to study the effect that these tradeoffs have in shaping pathogen evolution and emergence.

Name: How does noise affect the performance and evolutionary stability of synthetic circuits?
Content: Noise in signal processing affects the performance of a biological circuit at the biomolecular reaction timescale, even when its average behavior is expected to be the same. It can also lead to effects on the timescale of evolution, compromising the long-term performance of the system. We study mathematical models of biomolecular circuits to find more stable design strategies in synthetic biology.

Name: How do microplastic pollutants interact with human endocrine receptors?
Content: Machine learning methods for molecular interaction prediction can help us predict putative interactions between pollutants, particularly microplastic PFAS derivatives, and receptor proteins on our cells. This is particularly important in the context of endocrine receptors involved in reproductive biology.

Name: How does antibody-dependent enhancement affect dengue virus evolution?
Content: Antibody-dependent enhancement leads viruses such as dengue virus to have higher virulence and replication when hosts have developed imperfect antibody immunity against related strains. This molecular phenomenon has evolutionary implications that may explain patterns in the persistence and evolution of dengue virus serotypes.

Name: Genetic design of strains for upscaling in bioprocess engineering
Content: Scaling bioengineered processes to industrial production levels remains one of the more underappreciated and important challenges in biotechnology. By understanding differences in selective regimes found in different points of bioprocess development, we can design genetic systems and cellular factories that are more robust and effective for biomanufacturing.
